thread.title: Don't Abandon Dividend Stocks; Tweak Your Strategy Instead

author: Martin Tillier
title: Don't Abandon Dividend Stocks; Tweak Your Strategy Instead
text:
Shutterstock photo A few years ago, when it became clear that interest rates were going to stay "lower for longer" , there were many pundits advising investors to look to dividend paying stocks rather than bonds for yield. In the context of ultra-low rates and an economy that was still operating at well below capacity, that made perfect sense.
Dividend-paying stocks not only offered a yield comparable to, or in many cases higher than bonds, but also gave investors access to appreciation based on the continued recovery. Now, with the 10 Year Treasury Note yield approaching ten percent, that strategy looks a bit dated, but does that mean that investors should abandon dividend stocks?
The short answer is no. The more nuanced response is that while seeking yield from stocks rather than bonds still has advantages, investors should be looking at stocks with specific characteristics to take advantage of the current circumstances.
We can reasonably predict that rates will continue to move higher, hopefully in an orderly fashion. The Fed has signaled their intention to hike multiple times this year and will probably at some point start to reduce their balance sheet by selling securities that they hold. That will increase the downward pressure on fixed income prices and therefore the upward pressure on yields.
Higher yields in fixed income generally mean lower prices on stocks whose yield accounts for part of their value, so now may seem like a strange time to be recommending dividend payers.
That dynamic certainly applies to some traditional high dividend sectors such as telecoms and utilities, where the market is saturated or restricted enough to make it unlikely that the companies concerned will be able to benefit from the improved growth prospects that are in part triggering the rising rate environment.
Nor is energy a suitable sector to look for yield in that environment. A global shift away from fossil fuels and the unpredictable, volatile nature of oil and natural gas prices make sustained appreciation in those stocks unlikely over the long term.
Instead of those traditional sources of yield, investors need to look at companies that pay a decent dividend, but can still benefit from improved growth, and can handle a slightly more inflationary environment than we have come to expect over the last decade or so. Ideally, they should also have a strong international presence. The short-term risk of adjusting to higher U.S. interest rates will have less effect on companies who also operate in other global markets where rates remain low, and the changes to taxation of overseas profits combine with a low and still sinking dollar to exaggerate that advantage.
The obvious places to look for stocks that check all those boxes are in consumer discretionary and big tech stocks. Retail is still adjusting to the modern world, but established global brands in other under pressure areas, such as McDonalds ( MCD ), Starbucks ( SBUX ) and even the embattled Coca-Cola ( KO ) with projected twelve-month yields of 2.53, 2.16, and 3.35 percent respectively, fill the requirements.
However, my preference would be big tech, where growth can be achieved through strength in both business and consumer spending. The yields on some obvious candidates like Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Apple ( AAPL ) are too low to make them income vehicles, but other two other “old tech” names have good growth prospects and a yield of over 2.5%, Oracle ( ORCL ) and Cisco ( CSCO ). They would be my top choices, but there are plenty of names to look at in both sectors.
Whether you choose those or others, the point is not to abandon dividend-paying stocks just because we are looking at higher interest rates. Those from less traditional yield offering sectors offer the same benefits that dividend payers always have, which are income that can be withdrawn or re-invested and access to growth. Those things combined are valuable to any investor.
